- issue_comment created in `experiment-repo`#9 ("E9: the λ clip (synthetic sweep over b) and a strongest-valid-baseline column") by `experiment-repo`  > E9 and the strongest-valid-baseline columns are in `results/` (experiment-repo `main` 19eb276, paper-repo `dev` 5a96dad). Details of every column: `METHODS.md`, section "The λ clip".
  > 
  > **E9 (`clip_sweep.csv`, 61 synthetic cells; `clip_real.csv`, 57 real-pool cells; `experiments/exp9_clip.py`).** f ~ N(0,1), Y = b·f + 0.6·ε, truth 0, E[Y|f] affine (Δ = 0), so package vs unclipped PPI++ differ only by the clip. b ∈ {−0.5, 0, 0.8, 1.0, 1.2, 1.5, 2.0}; n ∈ {30, 100, 300, 1000, 3000} at N = 10⁴; N/n ∈ {1, 4} at n = 300; σ ∈ {0.3, 1.5} at n = 100, 1000 for b ≥ 1.2; 4000–8000 replicates; same draws for all arms; also both with λ fixed at its optimum (no estimation of λ).
  > - **Formula.** Exact excess of the packaged oracle over the optimum = (1/n − 1/M)(b − c)²Var f, c = clip(b, 0, M/N) (checked identical to the exact V(λ) difference to 1e-8). With λ fixed, the measured width ratio unclipped/package equals √(V(λ*)/V(clip λ*)) in all 61 cells (max abs difference 0.0011): b = 1.5, n = 100 → formula 0.785, measured 0.786; b = 2, n = 100 → 0.540 / 0.541; b = −0.5 (λ pinned at 0) → 0.771 / 0.771 at n = 100.
  > - **Condition.** No gain wherever b ≤ M/N (λ* ≤ 1): ratio 1.000 (oracle: exactly; estimated λ̂, n ≥ 300: within 0.0036). At n = 3000, N = 10⁴ (M/N = 1.3): b = 1.2 → 1.000, b = 1.5 → 0.983, b = 2 → 0.879. At N = n = 300 (M/N = 2) b = 2 → 1.000; N = 4n: b = 1.5 → 0.973, b = 2 → 0.852. b < 0 is pinned at the classical interval; the unclipped interval is 0.77–0.83 as wide (n = 100…3000).
  > - **With λ estimated** (what a user gets) the gain follows the formula only for n ≳ 300: the largest |measured − formula| is 0.131 at n = 30, 0.046 at n = 100, 0.014 at n = 300, 0.003 at n = 1000. At n = 30 the unclipped λ̂ is noisy: b = 1.0 → unclipped is 4.6% *wider* than the package; b = 1.2 → 1.9% wider although the formula says 4.9% narrower; b = 1.5, 2.0 → 0.888 / 0.654 (formula 0.773 / 0.522). So the clip helps at small n and hurts at large n. Coverage of both: 0.923–0.940 at n = 30, ≥ 0.942 at n ≥ 300, SE/SD of both ≈ 0.94–1.01.
  > - **Real sets (`clip_real.csv`; b, fraction λ̂ > 1, formula vs measured ratio unclipped/package over n).** gene_expression b = 1.152: fraction λ̂ > 1 = 0.71 / 0.86 / 0.96 / 0.98 / 0.93 / 0.00 at n = 30 / 100 / 300 / 500 / 1000 / 3000; formula 0.911 / 0.924 / 0.953 / 0.972 / 0.995 / 1.000; measured 0.990 / 0.955 / 0.962 / 0.977 / 0.996 / 1.000. census_income b = 1.375: formula 0.979 / 0.980 / 0.983 / 0.985 / 0.990 / 0.999, measured 0.978 / 0.976 / 0.982 / 0.985 / 0.990 / 0.999 (formula holds already at n = 30 there: its λ̂ is stable). alphafold b = 1.034 and the other six sets (b ≤ 0.985): formula 1.000 (no clip effect at any n ≥ 100 even though λ̂ > 1 in up to 53% of draws at alphafold n = 100); measured ratio unclipped/package > 1 at small n (alphafold n = 30 1.069, plankton 1.123, forest 1.038) = the noise of an unclipped λ̂, not the clip. So the packaged clip matters on exactly two of nine sets, gene_expression (largest at n ≈ 100–500) and census_income (a 1–2% effect, which already exists at n = 500). For Fig 6 use `clip_sweep.csv` (x = b, y = `width_ratio_unclip_over_pkg_oracle` and `…_unclip_over_pkg` at a fixed n/N; column `pred_width_ratio_unclip_over_pkg` is the formula) and `clip_real.csv` (`b`, same columns).
  > - `ladder.csv` has the step `clip` (unclipped PPI++, ratio to the package) between `ppipp` and `calib_T1` for the reference grid. The width ratio there is to the package; the arm-to-unclipped ratio is `ratio_vs_unclip` in `cells.csv` / `headline.csv`.
  > 
  > **Strongest valid baseline (`headline.csv`).** New columns: `baseline_used` (package | unclipped: the narrower of the two among those whose coverage is valid in the cell, Wilson upper limit ≥ 0.95; if neither is valid the narrower of the two with `baseline_valid` = 0), `baseline_package_valid`, `baseline_unclipped_valid`, `ratio_vs_valid_baseline` + `ratio_valid_lo/hi`, `classification_vs_valid_baseline`.
